cards.explanation: The answer is the Philistines. David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Metheg-ammah from their hand (2 Samuel 8:1). It's the first win on a list that gets long in a hurry.

The answer is spared. Two lengths of David's cord were for those to be put to death, and one length was for those to be spared (2 Samuel 8:2). This is a heavy moment, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there. The one-length group is the group that was spared.

The answer is tribute. The Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute (2 Samuel 8:2). Tribute is a payment made by people who are under someone's rule. So the verse tells you who they answer to and what they bring.
The answer is the Euphrates. King Hadadezer had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River (2 Samuel 8:3). Big river, big plans, friends. David defeated him anyway.

The answer is False. The text says David hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots (2 Samuel 8:4). So he kept only a hundred of them. It's a tough detail, friends, and the verse gives it plainly.

The answer is the Arameans of Damascus. They came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, and David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men (2 Samuel 8:5). That's a heavy number. Then in verse 6 the Arameans became subject to David.

The answer is the LORD. The passage says, “So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.” (2 Samuel 8:6). It says it right after the garrisons and the tribute. All those wins, and the passage gives the credit to Him.

The answer is Jerusalem. David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:7). Those shields changed owners and ended up in Jerusalem, friends.

The answer is his son Joram. King Toi of Hamath sent Joram to greet King David and bless him for defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi (2 Samuel 8:10). Joram came carrying articles of silver and gold and bronze. That's quite a greeting, friends.

The answer is True. King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued (2 Samuel 8:11). "These" means the silver, gold and bronze that Joram brought from King Toi. Verse 12 then lists where the other silver and gold came from.

The answer is a name. “And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.” (2 Samuel 8:13). The verse says exactly that, friends. It ties the name to his return.
The answer is False. Verse 14 says, “He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David.” (2 Samuel 8:14). The word is all. No Edomites are left out in that verse.

The answer is with justice and righteousness. The passage says David “…administered justice and righteousness for all his people…” (2 Samuel 8:15). After all the battles, this verse tells how he ruled. It's a quiet line after a loud chapter, friends.
